content.paragraph: In three dimensions there is a coordinate system, called cylindrical coordinates, that is similar to polar coordinates and gives convenient descriptions of some commonly occurring surfaces and solids. As we will see, some triple integrals are much easier to evaluate in cylindrical coordinates.

subsection.title: Cylindrical Coordinates
subsection.paragraph: In the cylindrical coordinate system, a point $$P$$ in three-dimensional space is represented by the ordered triple $$\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)$$ , where $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ are polar coordinates of the projection of $$P$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane and $$z$$ is the directed distance from the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane to $$P$$ . (See Figure 2.)

figure.alt_text: Two line segments and two points are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first line segment, labeled r, lies in the first quadrant of the x y plane, begins at the origin, and slopes downward to the right at an angle theta from the x axis until a point labeled (r, theta, 0). The second line segment, labeled z, is vertical and runs parallel to the z axis from (r, theta, 0) to a point labeled P(r, theta, z).

subsection.paragraph: Cylindrical coordinates are useful in problems that involve symmetry about an axis, and the $$z$$-axis is chosen to coincide with this axis of symmetry. For instance, the axis of the circular cylinder with Cartesian equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = c^{ 2}$$ is the $$z$$-axis. In cylindrical coordinates this cylinder has the very simple equation $$r = c$$ . (See Figure 4.) This is the reason for the name “cylindrical” coordinates. The graph of the equation $$\theta = c$$ is a vertical plane through the origin (see Figure 5), and the graph of the equation $$z = c$$ is a horizontal plane (see Figure 6).

problem.paragraph: Describe the surface whose equation in cylindrical coordinates is $$z = r$$ .

Solution The equation says that the $$z$$-value, or height, of each point on the surface is the same as $$r$$ , the distance from the point to the $$z$$-axis. Because $$\theta$$ doesn’t appear, it can vary. So any horizontal trace in the plane $$z = k{\left( {k > 0} \right)}$$ is a circle of radius $$k$$ . These traces suggest that the surface is a cone. This prediction can be confirmed by converting the equation into rectangular coordinates. From the first equation in (2) we have
We recognize the equation $$z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ (by comparison with Table 1 in Section 12.6) as being a circular cone whose axis is the $$z$$-axis (see Figure 7).

figure.caption: z = r , a cone
figure.alt_text: Two cones are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first cone has its tip at the origin and circular base parallel to the x y plane, with its center on the positive y axis. This cone has the positive y axis as its axis. The second cone has its tip at the origin and circular base parallel to the x y plane, with its center on the negative y axis. This cone has the negative y axis as its axis. Both the cones are of the same size and are mirror images of each other reflected over the x y plane.

Formula 4 is the formula for triple integration in cylindrical coordinates. It says that we convert a triple integral from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates by writing $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , leaving $$z$$ as it is, using the appropriate limits of integration for $$z$$ , $$r$$ , and $$\theta$$ , and replacing $$\mathit{dV}$$ by $$r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta$$ . (Figure 9 shows how to remember this.) It is worthwhile to use this formula when $$E$$ is a solid region easily described in cylindrical coordinates, and especially when the function $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ involves the expression $$x^{2} + y^{2}$$ .

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$E$$ is the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ and above the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane (see Figure 10).

figure.alt_text: The three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid is a paraboloid defined by z = 4 minus x^2 minus y^2, with its vertex on the positive z axis, opens downward until the x y plane. The circular base of the solid crosses the positive x and y axis at (2, 0, 0) and (0, 2, 0), respectively. Two vertical traces are drawn on the surface of the solid, both are parabolas opening downward sharing their vertices with the solid. The first trace has its arms falling on the first and third quadrant of the x y plane. The second trace has its arms falling on the second and fourth quadrant of the x y plane.

problem.paragraph: Solution Because $$E$$ is symmetric about the $$z$$-axis, we use cylindrical coordinates. In addition, cylindrical coordinates are appropriate because the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2} = 4 - (x^{2} + y^{2})$$ is easily expressed in cylindrical coordinates as $$z = 4 - r^{2}$$ . The paraboloid intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane in the circle $$r^{2} = 4$$ or, equivalently, $$r = 2$$ , so the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane is the disk $$r \leqslant 2$$ . Thus the region $$E$$ is given by

paragraph.math: $$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{4 - r^{2}}\left( r\cos\theta \right)^{2}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}(r^{3}\cos^{2}\theta)\rbrack(4 - r^{2})\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos^{2}\theta d\theta\int_{0}^{2}(4r^{3} - r^{5})\mathit{dr}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack \theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack r^{4} - \frac{1}{6}r^{6} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}(2\pi)(16 - \frac{32}{3}) = \frac{16}{3}\pi} \end{array}$$
